extracted_claims.claim_text: Evaluating creative language generation tasks like rap lyric ghostwriting requires a multifaceted evaluation methodology that considers fluency, coherence, and style matching.
evidence: Language generation tasks that seek to mimic human ability to use language creatively are difficult to evaluate, since one must consider creativity, style, and other non-trivial aspects of the generated text.
We believe that one of the reasons such tasks receive little attention is the lack of sound evaluation methodology, without which no task is well-defined, and no progress can be made.

Our evaluation results highlight the truly multifaceted nature of the ghostwriting task. While having a single measure of success is clearly desirable, our analysis shows the need for complementary metrics that evaluate different components of the overall task.
The lack of strong correlation supports the notion that different aspects of verse quality should be addressed separately. Moreover, the metrics are in fact complementary.

evidence: We introduce an improvement to the semi-automatic methodology used by Potash et al. (2015) that automatically penalizes repetitive text, which removes the need for manual intervention and enables a large-scale analysis.
In order to fully automate this method, we propose to handle highly repetitive text by weighting the rhyme density of a given verse by its entropy.

Lastly, we note that the fully automated methodology we propose is able to replicate the results of the previously available semi-automatic method for the rapper Fabolous, which was the only artist evaluated by Potash et al. extracted_claims.claim_text: Different evaluation metrics for creative language generation are complementary and show low correlation, emphasizing the need for a comprehensive approach.
evidence: The lack of strong correlation supports the notion that different aspects of verse quality should be addressed separately. Moreover, the metrics are in fact complementary. Even the measures of fluency and coherence, despite sharing a similar goal, have a relatively low correlation of 0.4.

Such low correlations emphasize our contribution, since other works (Barbieri et al., 2012; Wu, 2014; Malmi et al., 2015) do not provide a comprehensive evaluation methodology, and evaluate just one or two particular aspects.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Training Data Size Negatively Affects Coherence
extracted_claims.claim_text: The size of an artist's training data negatively correlates with the coherence score of generated lyrics, while fluency is less affected by dataset size.
evidence: Interestingly, the number of verses a rapper has in our dataset has a strong negative correlation with coherence score (cf. Table 4b). This can be explained by the following consideration: on iteration 16,000, the model for the authors with the smaller number of verses has seen the same verses more times than the model trained on a larger number of verses. Therefore, it is easier for the former to produce more coherent lyrics since it saw more of the same patterns. As a result, models trained on a larger number of verses have a lower coherence score. For example, Lil’ Wayne has the most verses in our data, and correspondingly, the model for his verse has the worst coherence score. Note that the fluency score does not have this negative correlation with the number of verses.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The LSTM model, trained on all verses from a given artist, is able to capture the artist’s “average” style, whereas authentic verses represent a random selection that are less likely, statistically speaking, to be similar to another random verse.
evidence: Furthermore, MatchA% is significantly higher for the LSTM model, which means that the annotators agreed on matching verses more frequently. We believe this means that the LSTM model, trained on all verses from a given artist, is able to capture the artist’s “average” style, whereas authentic verses represent a random selection that are less likely, statistically speaking, to be similar to another random verse.
uncertainty_flags: Interpretation of 'average' style needs clarification/validation.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Annotation Method Generalizable to Other Creative Tasks
extracted_claims.claim_text: The annotation method we propose for manual style evaluation can be used for other similar generation tasks, such as 'Deep Art' in computer vision.
evidence: Additionally, we believe that the annotation method we propose for manual style evaluation can be used for other similar generation tasks. One example is ’Deep Art’ work in the computer vision community that seeks to apply the style of a particular painting to other images (Gatys et al., 2015; Li and Wand, 2016). identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The goal of automatic ghostwriting is to create a system that can take as input a given artist’s work and generate similar yet unique lyrics.
supporting_evidence: The goal of automatic ghostwriting is therefore to create a system that can take as input a given artist’s work and generate similar yet unique lyrics.
Ghostwriting must produce text that is similar in style to the emulated artist, yet distinct in content.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the definition of 'ghostwriting' or its goals (similar yet unique) is not universally accepted or is incomplete, the entire evaluation framework built upon it may not be relevant or comprehensive for other interpretations of the task.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Annotating fluency and coherence at the line level is an effective and appropriate method for evaluating entire verses.
supporting_evidence: Even though our evaluation is for systems that produce entire verses, we follow the work of Wu (2014) and annotate fluency, as well as coherence, at the line level.

In contrast to previous approaches that evaluate whole verses, our evaluation methodology uses a fine-grained, line-by-line scheme, which makes it easier for human annotators, as they no longer need to evaluate the whole verse at once.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Line-level evaluation might miss emergent properties or overall flow/narrative coherence that only becomes apparent at the verse or stanza level. The sum of line-level scores might not accurately reflect verse-level quality.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Converting 'strongly fluent,' 'weakly fluent,' and 'not fluent' (and coherence equivalents) to 1, 0.5, and 0, respectively, allows for a valid continuous numeric score.
supporting_evidence: We convert the raw annotation results into a single score for each verse by treating the labels “strongly fluent”, “weakly fluent”, and “not fluent” as numeric values 1, 0.5, and 0, respectively.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: This assumes an interval scale for what is inherently an ordinal scale, potentially misrepresenting the actual difference between categories (e.g., is 'strongly fluent' truly twice as good as 'weakly fluent' in a linear sense?).

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The 1-of-4 forced-choice style matching task (one target artist verse, three distractors from other artists) effectively measures how well a generated verse captures the target artist's style.
supporting_evidence: In this annotation task, a user is presented with an evaluation verse and asked to compare it against four other verses. The goal is to pick the verse that is written in a similar style. One of the four choices is always a verse from the same artist that was used to generate the verse being evaluated. The other three verses are chosen from the remaining artists in our dataset.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: The choice of distractors (random other artists) might influence the perceived similarity. The task might measure general 'rap-ness' or 'artist-ness' rather than specific stylistic nuances.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Rhyme density, as defined and calculated by the chosen tool, is an objective and sufficient metric for evaluating an artist's rhyming style.
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Section 4.2 Stylistic Similarity via Rhyme Density of Lyrics
supporting_evidence: We use the rhyme density method proposed by Hirjee and Brown (2010a) to evaluate how well the generated verse models an artist’s style. The point of an effective system is not to produce arbitrary rhymes: it is to produce rhyme types and rhyme frequency similar to the target artist. Distilling the various rhyme metrics offered by the tool, we focus on rhyme density...
Therefore, an objective automatic methodology is desirable. Since this tool is trained on a distinct corpus of lyrics, it can provide a ”uniform” experience and give an impartial and objective score.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Rhyme density might not capture all relevant aspects of rhyming style (e.g., complexity, unexpectedness, semantic interplay). The 'impartial and objective score' relies on the tool's internal validity and generalizability.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Weighting rhyme density by token-level entropy effectively penalizes false positive rhymes due to repetitive text and fully automates the process.
supporting_evidence: In order to fully automate this method, we propose to handle highly repetitive text by weighting the rhyme density of a given verse by its entropy. More specifically, for a given verse, we calculate entropy at the token level and divide by total number of tokens in that verse. Verses with highly repetitive text will have a low entropy, which results in down-weighting the rhyme density of verses that produce false positive rhymes due to their repetitive text.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Entropy might not perfectly capture all forms of undesirable repetition or might inadvertently penalize legitimate stylistic repetition. The effectiveness of this specific weighting scheme needs empirical validation beyond just enabling automation.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Using regression lines on rhyme density and maximum similarity scores across training iterations effectively identifies the 'optimal' balance point for ghostwriting (low similarity at target rhyme density).
supporting_evidence: Therefore, our goal is to evaluate the value of the maximum similarity at the point where the rhyme density has the value of the target artist. In order to accomplish this, we follow Potash et al. (2015) and plot the values of rhyme density and maximum similarity obtained at different points during model training. We use regression lines for these points to identify the value of the maximum similarity line at the point where the rhyme density line has the value of the target artist.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: The linearity or appropriateness of regression for these metrics across training iterations might be questionable. The 'optimal' point defined by this method might not align with human perception of good ghostwriting.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: There is a correspondence between higher n-gram length and higher LSTM training iterations in terms of model 'fit' to training data, allowing for comparison.
supporting_evidence: We see a correspondence between higher n and higher iteration: as both increase, the models become more ‘fit’ to the training data.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: This correspondence might be an oversimplification. The learning dynamics and capabilities of an n-gram model and an LSTM are fundamentally different, and equating their 'fit' based on these parameters might lead to invalid comparisons.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Native English-speaking rap fans are suitable annotators, and their subjective judgments, even with low IAA for some tasks, are valid for evaluating creative language.
supporting_evidence: Each line is annotated by two annotators.

Raw inter-annotator agreement (IAA) for fluency annotation was 0.67. For coherence annotation, the IAA was 0.43. We believe coherence has a lower agreement because it is more semantic, as opposed to syntactic, in nature, causing it to be more subjective. Note that while the agreement is relatively low, it is expected, given the subjective nature of the task. For example, Wu (2014) report similar agreement values for the fluency annotation they perform.
Each page was annotated twice, by native English-speaking rap fans.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Low IAA, especially for coherence and style, indicates significant subjectivity. While acknowledged, it raises questions about the reliability and generalizability of the manual scores. Different annotator pools might yield different results.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The heuristic preprocessing steps (removing metadata, repetition markup, chorus lines, filtering short verses) result in a clean and representative dataset of actual rap verses.
supporting_evidence: We removed the metadata, line repetiton markup, and chorus lines, and tokenized the lyrics using the NLTK library (Bird et al., 2009). Since the preprocessing was done heuristically, the resulting dataset may still contain some text that is not actual verse, but rather dialogue or chorus lines. We therefore filter out all verses that are shorter than 20 tokens.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: The acknowledgment of potential remaining non-verse text suggests that the training data for the models, and thus the basis for evaluation, might be noisy or not perfectly representative of 'rap lyrics'.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper addresses the critical challenge of evaluating creative language generation, specifically focusing on rap lyric ghostwriting. It posits that existing evaluation methods are insufficient for creative tasks, necessitating a multifaceted approach. The core argument unfolds by first establishing this problem, then proposing a comprehensive evaluation methodology combining manual assessments (fluency, coherence, style matching) and automated metrics (uniqueness, rhyme density with an improved repetition penalty). This methodology is then empirically applied to an LSTM-based ghostwriting model, demonstrating its utility in revealing model strengths and weaknesses. The paper also contributes a publicly available, annotated rap lyric corpus. The logical flow is generally strong, moving from problem identification to solution proposal, empirical validation, and derived insights. However, the reliability of some manual metrics due to low inter-annotator agreement and certain methodological assumptions warrant closer examination.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Creative language generation tasks (e.g., rap lyric ghostwriting) are difficult to evaluate due to non-trivial aspects like creativity and style, leading to a lack of sound evaluation methodology (C1).
G1: To address P1, the paper aims to develop a comprehensive, quantifiable evaluation methodology for rap lyric ghostwriting (C2).

M1: The proposed methodology includes manual evaluation of fluency, coherence (line-level, ordinal-to-numeric scoring), and style matching (forced-choice task comparing generated vs. authentic verses) (C1, C2).

M2: The methodology also includes automated evaluation of uniqueness (max similarity to training data) and stylistic similarity (rhyme density, improved with an entropy-based repetition penalty) (C2, C5).
M3: A publicly available corpus of rap lyrics with stylistic similarity annotations is created to support this evaluation and future research (C4).
A1: The methodology is applied to an LSTM-based rap lyric ghostwriting model to demonstrate its effectiveness.

F1: The developed methodology effectively showcases the strengths and weaknesses of generative models, such as the LSTM, revealing challenges like maintaining coherence with large training datasets and capturing general artist style (C3).
F2: Different evaluation metrics for creative language generation are complementary and show low correlation, emphasizing the need for a comprehensive approach (C6).
F3: The size of an artist's training data negatively correlates with the coherence score of generated lyrics, while fluency is less affected (C7).
F4: The LSTM model captures an 'average' artist style, which can lead to higher match rates in style evaluation compared to authentic verses (C8).
F5: The fully automated repetition penalty improves existing semi-automatic evaluation methods and generalizes better than baseline models (C5).
I1: The evaluation methodology provides an explicit, quantifiable foundation for the ghostwriting task, allowing for a deeper understanding of its goals and future research directions (C2, C3).
S1: The annotation method for manual style evaluation is speculated to be generalizable to other similar generation tasks, such as 'Deep Art' in computer vision (C9).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a comprehensive, multifaceted evaluation methodology for creative language generation, specifically focusing on rap lyric ghostwriting. It reconstructs the reasoning that existing evaluation methods for creative NLG are insufficient due to their narrow focus, necessitating a new framework that considers fluency, coherence, and style matching. The methodology combines manual human annotation (for fluency, coherence, and style matching via a 1-of-4 forced choice task) with automated metrics (modified TF-IDF for uniqueness and entropy-weighted rhyme density for stylistic similarity). The paper then applies this methodology to evaluate an LSTM-based rap lyric ghostwriting model and an n-gram baseline, deriving insights into model performance, such as the negative correlation between training data size and coherence. A key contribution is the release of a new rap lyric corpus with stylistic similarity annotations. The paper argues that the low correlation between its proposed metrics underscores the need for a comprehensive approach, and that the automated repetition penalty improves upon prior semi-automatic methods.

identified_claims.claim_text: Evaluating creative language generation tasks like rap lyric ghostwriting requires a multifaceted evaluation methodology that considers fluency, coherence, and style matching.
evidence: Language generation tasks that seek to mimic human ability to use language creatively are difficult to evaluate, since one must consider creativity, style, and other non-trivial aspects of the generated text.
We believe that one of the reasons such tasks receive little attention is the lack of sound evaluation methodology, without which no task is well-defined, and no progress can be made.

Our evaluation results highlight the truly multifaceted nature of the ghostwriting task. While having a single measure of success is clearly desirable, our analysis shows the need for complementary metrics that evaluate different components of the overall task.
The lack of strong correlation supports the notion that different aspects of verse quality should be addressed separately. Moreover, the metrics are in fact complementary.

identified_claims.claim_text: The proposed manual and automated evaluation methods provide a quantifiable foundation for analyzing system performance in rap lyric ghostwriting.
evidence: The goal of this paper is to develop evaluation methods for one such task, ghostwriting of rap lyrics, and to provide an explicit, quantifiable foundation for the goals and future directions of this task.

Overall, the evaluation methodology we present provides an explicit, quantifiable foundation for the ghostwriting task, allowing for a deeper understanding of the task’s goals and future research directions.
In this paper, we have presented a comprehensive evaluation methodology for the task of ghostwriting rap lyrics, which captures complementary aspects of this task and its goals.

identified_claims.claim_text: The developed methodology can effectively showcase the strengths and weaknesses of generative models, such as an LSTM, revealing challenges like maintaining coherence with large training datasets and capturing general artist style.
evidence: the full set of evaluation metrics is able to showcase the LSTM model’s strengths and weaknesses. The coherence evaluation demonstrates the difficulty of incorporating large amounts of training data into the LSTM model, which intuitively would be desirable to create a flexible ghostwriting model. The style matching experiments suggest that the LSTM is effective at capturing an artist’s general style.
Interestingly, the number of verses a rapper has in our dataset has a strong negative correlation with coherence score (cf. Table 4b).
As can be seen from Table 2, the Match% score suggests that the LSTM-generated verses are able to capture the style of the artist as well as the original verses.

identified_claims.claim_text: A publicly available corpus of rap lyrics with stylistic similarity annotations is provided to support future research.
evidence: Finally, we build a corpus of lyrics for 13 rap artists, each with his own unique style, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the LSTM model performance using the new evaluation methodology. The corpus includes style matching annotation for select verses in dataset, which can form a gold standard for future work on automatic representation of similarity between artists’ styles. The resulting rap lyric dataset is publicly available from the authors’ website.
We have made the dataset publicly available3.

identified_claims.claim_text: The fully automated repetition penalty improves existing semi-automatic evaluation methods and generalizes better than baseline models.
identified_claims.section_anchor: Section 1 Introduction, Section 4.2 Automated Evaluation, Section 7 Discussion, Section 8 Conclusion
evidence: We introduce an improvement to the semi-automatic methodology used by Potash et al. (2015) that automatically penalizes repetitive text, which removes the need for manual intervention and enables a large-scale analysis.
In order to fully automate this method, we propose to handle highly repetitive text by weighting the rhyme density of a given verse by its entropy.

Lastly, we note that the fully automated methodology we propose is able to replicate the results of the previously available semi-automatic method for the rapper Fabolous, which was the only artist evaluated by Potash et al. (2015). Furthermore, the results of automated evaluation for the 11 artists confirm that the LSTM model generalizes better than the baseline model.

identified_claims.claim_text: Different evaluation metrics for creative language generation are complementary and show low correlation, emphasizing the need for a comprehensive approach.
evidence: The lack of strong correlation supports the notion that different aspects of verse quality should be addressed separately. Moreover, the metrics are in fact complementary. Even the measures of fluency and coherence, despite sharing a similar goal, have a relatively low correlation of 0.4.

Such low correlations emphasize our contribution, since other works (Barbieri et al., 2012; Wu, 2014; Malmi et al., 2015) do not provide a comprehensive evaluation methodology, and evaluate just one or two particular aspects.

identified_claims.claim_label: Training Data Size Negatively Affects Coherence
identified_claims.claim_text: The size of an artist's training data negatively correlates with the coherence score of generated lyrics, while fluency is less affected by dataset size.
evidence: Interestingly, the number of verses a rapper has in our dataset has a strong negative correlation with coherence score (cf. Table 4b). This can be explained by the following consideration: on iteration 16,000, the model for the authors with the smaller number of verses has seen the same verses more times than the model trained on a larger number of verses. Therefore, it is easier for the former to produce more coherent lyrics since it saw more of the same patterns. As a result, models trained on a larger number of verses have a lower coherence score. For example, Lil’ Wayne has the most verses in our data, and correspondingly, the model for his verse has the worst coherence score. Note that the fluency score does not have this negative correlation with the number of verses.

identified_claims.claim_text: The LSTM model, trained on all verses from a given artist, is able to capture the artist’s “average” style, whereas authentic verses represent a random selection that are less likely, statistically speaking, to be similar to another random verse.
evidence: Furthermore, MatchA% is significantly higher for the LSTM model, which means that the annotators agreed on matching verses more frequently. We believe this means that the LSTM model, trained on all verses from a given artist, is able to capture the artist’s “average” style, whereas authentic verses represent a random selection that are less likely, statistically speaking, to be similar to another random verse.

evidence: Additionally, we believe that the annotation method we propose for manual style evaluation can be used for other similar generation tasks. One example is ’Deep Art’ work in the computer vision community that seeks to apply the style of a particular painting to other images (Gatys et al., 2015; Li and Wand, 2016). concerns.title: Validity of Ordinal to Interval Scale Conversion
concerns.description: The conversion of ordinal human ratings ('strongly fluent', 'weakly fluent', 'not fluent') to a continuous numeric scale (1, 0.5, 0) assumes an equal interval between categories (A3). This is a strong assumption that may not hold true for subjective human perception, potentially misrepresenting the actual differences in quality and affecting statistical analysis based on these scores. For example, the difference between 'strongly fluent' and 'weakly fluent' might not be perceived as exactly equal to the difference between 'weakly fluent' and 'not fluent'.
evidence: A3: Converting 'strongly fluent,' 'weakly fluent,' and 'not fluent' (and coherence equivalents) to 1, 0.5, and 0, respectively, allows for a valid continuous numeric score.

Section 6.1 Fluency/Coherence: 'We convert the raw annotation results into a single score for each verse by treating the labels “strongly fluent”, “weakly fluent”, and “not fluent” as numeric values 1, 0.5, and 0, respectively.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Justify the linearity assumption for the scoring scale, or explore alternative non-parametric statistical methods for analysis, or use a more robust scaling method (e.g., Rasch model) if a continuous scale is critical.

concerns.title: Impact of Low Inter-Annotator Agreement (IAA)
concerns.description: The reported raw IAA for coherence (0.43) and style matching (ranging from 0% to 72.7% for MatchA%, with average raw agreement 42.3% for authentic and 34.1% for generated) is low (A9). While acknowledged as expected for subjective tasks, low agreement significantly impacts the reliability and generalizability of the manual evaluation results. It raises questions about whether the 'ground truth' established by annotators is consistent enough to draw robust conclusions about model performance, especially for coherence and specific stylistic nuances.
evidence: A9: Native English-speaking rap fans are suitable annotators, and their subjective judgments, even with low IAA for some tasks, are valid for evaluating creative language.

Section 6.1 Fluency/Coherence: 'Raw inter-annotator agreement (IAA) for fluency annotation was 0.67. For coherence annotation, the IAA was 0.43. We believe coherence has a lower agreement because it is more semantic, as opposed to syntactic, in nature, causing it to be more subjective.'
Table 2: 'Raw agreement %' for style matching, averaging 42.3% (authentic) and 34.1% (generated).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a more thorough discussion of the implications of low IAA on the validity of conclusions, especially for coherence and style. Consider methods to improve agreement (e.g., more detailed guidelines, training, adjudication) or analyze results with agreement levels as a variable. Explore whether higher agreement subsets of data yield different insights.

concerns.title: Robustness of Automated Rhyme Density and Entropy Weighting
concerns.description: The automated stylistic similarity relies on a specific external rhyme detection tool (Hirjee and Brown, 2010a) and an entropy-based weighting scheme to penalize repetition (A5, A6). The robustness of this approach depends heavily on the external tool's generalizability to diverse rap styles and the effectiveness of entropy as a proxy for 'undesirable' repetition. It's unclear if entropy weighting might inadvertently penalize legitimate stylistic repetition (e.g., hooks, ad-libs) common in rap, or if the tool's training corpus aligns sufficiently with the diverse rap styles evaluated. The paper states the tool is 'trained on a distinct corpus of lyrics' but does not elaborate on its compatibility.
evidence: A5: Rhyme density, as defined and calculated by the chosen tool, is an objective and sufficient metric for evaluating an artist's rhyming style.
A6: Weighting rhyme density by token-level entropy effectively penalizes false positive rhymes due to repetitive text and fully automates the process.

Section 4.2 Stylistic Similarity via Rhyme Density of Lyrics: 'Since this tool is trained on a distinct corpus of lyrics, it can provide a ”uniform” experience and give an impartial and objective score.'
Section 4.2 Automated Evaluation: 'In order to fully automate this method, we propose to handle highly repetitive text by weighting the rhyme density of a given verse by its entropy.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide more details on the external rhyme detection tool's characteristics (e.g., training data, known biases). Empirically validate the entropy weighting scheme against human judgments of repetition quality, or explore alternative methods for identifying and penalizing undesirable repetition.

concerns.title: Validity of 'Optimal' Point for Uniqueness and Similarity Trade-off
concerns.description: The method for merging uniqueness and similarity relies on plotting regression lines for rhyme density and maximum similarity across training iterations to find an 'optimal' point (A7). The assumption that a linear regression accurately captures the relationship between these metrics across training and that the intersection point represents a human-perceived 'optimal' balance is not strongly justified. The dynamics of model training and the subjective nature of 'optimal' ghostwriting might not be adequately captured by this linear approximation.
evidence: A7: Using regression lines on rhyme density and maximum similarity scores across training iterations effectively identifies the 'optimal' balance point for ghostwriting (low similarity at target rhyme density).

Section 4.2 Merging Uniqueness and Similarity: 'We use regression lines for these points to identify the value of the maximum similarity line at the point where the rhyme density line has the value of the target artist.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide empirical or theoretical justification for the use of linear regression in this context. Consider exploring non-linear models or alternative definitions of the 'optimal' trade-off point, potentially involving human feedback on the perceived quality of verses at different points along the training trajectory.

concerns.title: Equivalence of N-gram Length and LSTM Iterations for Comparison
concerns.description: The paper assumes a correspondence between higher n-gram length and higher LSTM training iterations in terms of model 'fit' to training data to enable comparison (A8). This is a significant simplification, as n-gram models and LSTMs have fundamentally different architectures and learning mechanisms. Equating their 'fit' based on these disparate parameters might lead to invalid comparisons and conclusions about their relative performance, especially regarding generalization and stylistic capture.
evidence: A8: There is a correspondence between higher n-gram length and higher LSTM training iterations in terms of model 'fit' to training data, allowing for comparison.
Section 5 Lyric Generation Experiments: 'We see a correspondence between higher n and higher iteration: as both increase, the models become more ‘fit’ to the training data.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a more rigorous justification or empirical validation for the assumed correspondence between n-gram length and LSTM training iterations. Alternatively, consider a different baseline comparison that does not rely on this potentially flawed equivalence, or explicitly discuss the limitations of this comparison method.

concerns.title: Potential Noise in Heuristically Preprocessed Dataset
concerns.description: The dataset preprocessing was done heuristically, and the authors acknowledge that the resulting dataset 'may still contain some text that is not actual verse, but rather dialogue or chorus lines' (A10). This potential noise in the training data could impact the models' ability to learn genuine rap lyric patterns and subsequently affect the validity of the evaluation results. The filtering of verses shorter than 20 tokens might not be sufficient to remove all non-verse content, and the specific impact of this noise on the LSTM's learning and generated output is not thoroughly analyzed.
evidence: A10: The heuristic preprocessing steps (removing metadata, repetition markup, chorus lines, filtering short verses) result in a clean and representative dataset of actual rap verses.

Section 3 Dataset: 'Since the preprocessing was done heuristically, the resulting dataset may still contain some text that is not actual verse, but rather dialogue or chorus lines. We therefore filter out all verses that are shorter than 20 tokens.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Quantify the amount of potential noise remaining in the dataset after preprocessing. Discuss the potential impact of this noise on model training and evaluation results. Consider more robust or manually verified preprocessing for a subset of the data to assess the quality.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a comprehensive evaluation methodology for rap lyric ghostwriting, a task within creative language generation. Its core contribution lies in extending and integrating existing, disparate evaluation approaches into a unified, multifaceted framework. Specifically, it refines manual evaluation by considering fluency, coherence, and style matching, building upon prior work that focused on individual aspects (e.g., Wu (2014), Barbieri et al. (2012)). A key incremental improvement is the full automation of a semi-automatic repetition penalty metric, originally proposed by Potash et al. (2015), by weighting rhyme density with token-level entropy. This significantly enhances the scalability and objectivity of stylistic evaluation. Furthermore, the paper contributes a new, publicly available rap lyric corpus annotated for stylistic similarity, which is an incremental but valuable resource for future research in this specific domain. The empirical analysis of an LSTM model using this new methodology provides insights into the model's strengths and weaknesses, particularly regarding coherence with large datasets and capturing 'average' artist style, thus incrementally advancing the understanding of generative models for creative tasks. The paper's argument for the necessity of complementary metrics, supported by observed low correlations, reorganizes the paradigm of evaluation for creative NLG by advocating for a holistic approach rather than reliance on single metrics.

identified_claims.claim_label: Training Data Size Negatively Affects Coherence
identified_claims.claim_text: The size of an artist's training data negatively correlates with the coherence score of generated lyrics, while fluency is less affected by dataset size.
evidence: Interestingly, the number of verses a rapper has in our dataset has a strong negative correlation with coherence score (cf. Table 4b). This can be explained by the following consideration: on iteration 16,000, the model for the authors with the smaller number of verses has seen the same verses more times than the model trained on a larger number of verses. Therefore, it is easier for the former to produce more coherent lyrics since it saw more of the same patterns. As a result, models trained on a larger number of verses have a lower coherence score. For example, Lil’ Wayne has the most verses in our data, and correspondingly, the model for his verse has the worst coherence score. Note that the fluency score does not have this negative correlation with the number of verses.

identified_claims.claim_text: The LSTM model, trained on all verses from a given artist, is able to capture the artist’s “average” style, whereas authentic verses represent a random selection that are less likely, statistically speaking, to be similar to another random verse.
evidence: Furthermore, MatchA% is significantly higher for the LSTM model, which means that the annotators agreed on matching verses more frequently. We believe this means that the LSTM model, trained on all verses from a given artist, is able to capture the artist’s “average” style, whereas authentic verses represent a random selection that are less likely, statistically speaking, to be similar to another random verse.

concerns.title: Impact of Low Inter-Annotator Agreement on Manual Metrics
concerns.description: The reported low inter-annotator agreement (IAA) for coherence (0.43) and the raw agreement for style matching (average 42.3%) raise concerns about the reliability and robustness of these subjective manual evaluations. While acknowledged, the implications of such low agreement on the validity and generalizability of the derived scores and conclusions should be discussed more thoroughly.
evidence: Raw inter-annotator agreement (IAA) for fluency annotation was 0.67. For coherence annotation, the IAA was 0.43. We believe coherence has a lower agreement because it is more semantic, as opposed to syntactic, in nature, causing it to be more subjective. Note that while the agreement is relatively low, it is expected, given the subjective nature of the task. For example, Wu (2014) report similar agreement values for the fluency annotation they perform.

Raw agreement for style annotation, which corresponds to the percentage of times annotators picked the same verse (whether or not they are correct) is shown in the column 'Raw agreement %' in Table 2.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss the limitations imposed by low IAA more explicitly, particularly for coherence and style matching. Explore methods to improve agreement in future work (e.g., more detailed guidelines, annotator training, different annotation paradigms) or provide sensitivity analysis on how varying interpretations might affect conclusions.

concerns.title: Validity of Ordinal to Interval Scale Conversion
concerns.description: The conversion of ordinal annotation labels ('strongly fluent', 'weakly fluent', 'not fluent') to a continuous numeric scale (1, 0.5, 0) assumes an interval scale for these subjective judgments. This simplification might misrepresent the actual perceptual differences between categories and could affect the validity of aggregated scores and subsequent statistical analyses.
evidence: We convert the raw annotation results into a single score for each verse by treating the labels “strongly fluent”, “weakly fluent”, and “not fluent” as numeric values 1, 0.5, and 0, respectively.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Justify the choice of linear scaling for ordinal data, or consider alternative non-parametric statistical methods that are more appropriate for ordinal scales. Acknowledge this assumption and its potential impact on the interpretation of results.

For automated metrics, more details on the external rhyme detection tool and empirical validation of the entropy weighting scheme are recommended, along with justification for the linear regression approach for the 'optimal' point. epistemic_limits: The inherent subjectivity of creative language generation tasks, particularly for aspects like coherence and style, poses a fundamental epistemic limit, as evidenced by consistently low inter-annotator agreement. This suggests that a single, universally agreed-upon 'ground truth' for these aspects may be elusive.

The operationalization of abstract concepts such as 'average style' or the 'optimal balance' between uniqueness and similarity relies on specific methodological choices (e.g., regression lines, entropy weighting) that may not fully capture the nuanced human perception of these complex qualities.

While the methodology is comprehensive for rap lyric ghostwriting, its direct transferability and validity to other creative domains (e.g., 'Deep Art') remain speculative without empirical validation, indicating a current epistemic boundary.

The heuristic nature of dataset preprocessing introduces a limit on the certainty that the training and evaluation data perfectly represent 'actual rap verses' without residual noise, potentially affecting the generalizability of findings.

The assumption of equivalence between n-gram length and LSTM iterations for model 'fit' introduces an epistemic limit on the direct comparability of insights derived from these fundamentally different model architectures.

- The paper successfully argues for and implements a multifaceted evaluation methodology for creative language generation, explicitly demonstrating through empirical correlation analysis that different metrics are complementary and necessary due to their low inter-correlation.
